c1.story:
Walk into a truck dealership in Namakkal, a jewellery-heavy household in Thrissur, or a consumer-electronics store in Pune during Diwali, and ask who is financing the purchase. Very often it is not a bank. It is an NBFC, a non-banking financial company: a lender with a licence to lend but not to take your savings account.

That one missing permission shapes everything. Without cheap deposits, an NBFC has to borrow from banks and the bond market at wholesale rates, so it can only make money by lending to people banks find too small, too risky or too slow to serve, and charging them for it. A used-truck owner with patchy paperwork. A shopkeeper with no audited accounts. A first-time buyer of a phone on EMI.

But the label NBFC covers four very different animals, and the card sorts them into four doors. The retail and vehicle lenders, Bajaj Finance, Shriram Finance, Cholamandalam, Tata Capital, are the classic version: branches, dealer desks and apps, high rates, high growth, and a constant battle to keep defaults in check. The government infrastructure lenders, Power Finance Corporation, REC and Indian Railway Finance Corporation, are almost the opposite: they borrow nearly as cheaply as the government and lend huge sums to state power utilities and the railways at thin spreads. The gold and housing specialists lend against collateral you can touch: jewellery in a vault, or a house. And the holding companies, Bajaj Finserv, Bajaj Holdings, Jio Financial, Aditya Birla Capital, own pieces of lenders, insurers and brokers rather than lending much themselves.

Same rate cut, four different stories: growth for one door, cheaper bonds for another, nothing much for the gold lender, and a sum-of-parts sum for the holding company.

That is why the door matters before the numbers do. Comparing Bajaj Finance's margin with REC's is like comparing a restaurant's markup with a wholesaler's. Both are right; they are just different businesses.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each from top to bottom and give the bar the most attention.

  • The name and the line under it tell you who borrows and how the loan is sold: dealers and apps for retail, sovereign-like bonds for the government lenders, collateral for gold and housing, and ownership stakes for the holding companies.
  • The tickers are listed names that sit mostly behind each door; click one to open its stock page. Note that Bajaj Housing Finance and L&T Finance are placed in the third tile, and that Bajaj appears in three tiles: the lender, the housing arm and the holding companies above them.
  • The profit bar shows how much of the profit the business gets to keep. Retail and vehicle lenders sit at high: their customers do not shop around on rate, so a good lender keeps a fat spread. Every other door sits at medium, each for a different reason. The government lenders keep a thin but very safe spread. The gold and housing specialists face banks moving into their patch. The holding companies earn only what their subsidiaries earn, and the market applies a discount on top.
  • The bet line tells you what you are underwriting: growth with controlled defaults, the government's capex pipeline, gold and housing, or the businesses underneath.

The so-what below is the practical rule: value each door on its own yardstick, growth and credit quality, dividend yield, the gold price, or the sum of the parts. Using the wrong yardstick is the commonest mistake made with this sector.

c2.story:
An NBFC is a money wholesaler turned retailer. It buys money in bulk and sells it in small packets. Follow a rupee through the five stations and you will see where the margin is made and where it can be lost.

The first station is borrowing, and it is the only one an NBFC does not control. The money comes from banks as term loans, from mutual funds and insurers buying its bonds and commercial paper, from selling pools of loans to banks, and for a few, from public deposits. Every rupee arrives at whatever price these lenders choose to charge, and that price depends on the NBFC's credit rating and on how nervous the market is that month.

The second station is finding the customer. This is where the best NBFCs earn their keep. Bajaj Finance built a machine that signs up shoppers at the point of sale and then sells them a second and third loan. Shriram built a network that understands used trucks better than any bank. Muthoot built branches across the south where a family can walk in with a necklace and walk out with cash in under an hour.

The third station is underwriting: deciding who gets the loan and at what rate, often for borrowers with thin or no credit history. Here the government lenders are a different world: PFC and REC lend to state utilities, where the question is less whether a borrower is good and more whether the state will stand behind it.

The fourth station is collections, and in this business it is a physical job: field staff visiting borrowers, repossessing trucks, auctioning gold. The fifth station recycles capital, selling insurance and cards to existing borrowers and selling loan pools to banks to free up funding.

No foreign rival appears here. The rival is the bank down the road, which has cheaper money and waits for a segment to look safe before moving in.
c2.read:
Read the top row from left to right: borrowed money comes in at the first box and goes out as loans, gets collected and recycled.

  • Each box names the station, what happens there and who stands there. Notice the change from the first box to the rest. Station one is filled with banks, mutual funds, insurers and bond investors. Every box after that names listed NBFCs.
  • The band row makes this visual. The first cell, banks and the bond market, is not coloured: it belongs to someone else. The next three cells are coloured as Indian listed: sourcing, underwriting and collections all belong to the NBFCs. The last cell, cross-sell and capital recycling, is shared with banks, which buy the loan pools and partner on products.
  • No rival row is drawn, because no foreign player stands in this kitchen. The competition is domestic: banks and fintechs.

The note below the diagram adds the geography: gold lending in Kerala and the south, vehicle finance in the south and west, microfinance in the east and south. That matters when a state passes a lending law or a region has a bad monsoon.

Now read the so-what line, because it is the most important sentence on this card. The one uncoloured cell at the start, borrowing, is the station that can kill an NBFC. After IL&FS defaulted in 2018, banks and mutual funds stopped lending to the sector within weeks, and every station downstream seized up. When you look at any NBFC, look at that first cell for it: who lends to it, at what rating, and for how long.

c3.story:
Banks like customers who look good on paper: salaried, documented, with a long credit history. NBFCs make their living from everyone else. That is not a polite way of saying they lend to bad borrowers. It is a way of saying they lend to borrowers whose quality a bank's form cannot see.

Take the truck owner. He may own two old trucks, earn well in a good freight season and file no formal accounts. A bank sees risk. Shriram Finance, which has financed used commercial vehicles for decades, sees a borrower whose income depends on freight rates and diesel prices, whose collateral it knows how to value and repossess, and whose repayment it can collect in person.

Or the gold owner. Indian households hold a vast amount of gold jewellery, and when a farmer needs money before sowing or a family faces a hospital bill, a gold loan is the fastest credit in the country. The loan is small, short and backed by metal in the lender's vault. When gold rallies, as it did through 2025, each necklace supports a bigger loan.

Then there are consumers buying phones and fridges on EMI, small businesses borrowing against their shop or property, home buyers who are self-employed or buying an affordable flat, and women in rural self-help groups taking small microfinance loans. Each group pays more than a bank customer would, and each defaults more when its own world turns sour: microfinance borrowers when they borrow from too many lenders at once, consumers when urban jobs wobble.

And then there is the giant at the end of the list: state power utilities and government projects. These borrowers take long loans in thousands of crores for power plants, transmission lines, renewables and railway rolling stock. They are not underserved by banks so much as too big and too long-dated for them.

The NBFC's customer is the one the bank skipped. That is where the extra yield comes from, and where the extra risk lives.
c3.read:
Each tile is a borrower group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who borrows.
  • The second line is what they take: personal and consumer-durable loans, vehicle and tractor loans, business loans and loans against property, gold loans, home loans, infrastructure loans, microfinance.
  • The third line is what moves them, which is your watch list outside finance: urban jobs and festival spending, freight rates and fuel prices, GST collections, the gold price, interest rates and property prices, budget capex and state finances, rural incomes and state lending laws.

Sort the tiles by how the loan is protected. Gold, vehicles, homes and property are secured: if the borrower stops paying, the lender has something to sell. Consumer and microfinance loans are unsecured: the lender has only the borrower's willingness and ability to pay. The government tile is secured in a different sense, by the state's implicit backing.

Then map the tiles to the doors on card one. The retail and vehicle lenders draw on the first three tiles. The gold and housing specialists live in the gold and home-buyer tiles. The government lenders live almost entirely in the power utilities tile. Microfinance sits mostly with small finance banks and specialist lenders, but several diversified NBFCs have exposure to it too.

The so-what line is the summary: the customer banks underserve is the source of both the higher yield and the higher default rate. When you read an NBFC's loan mix, you are reading its risk.

c4.story:
An NBFC's profit and loss statement looks like a bank's with the safety net removed. Interest paid is the raw material, not a financing charge. The spread between what the NBFC earns on loans and what it pays for borrowed money is its gross margin. And then two lines decide whether that spread becomes profit: what it costs to run the machine, and how many loans fail.

Start with the cost of funds. A bank pays very little on savings accounts. An NBFC pays bond-market rates on everything, and those rates depend on its credit rating. That has a sharp consequence. When the RBI cuts rates, an NBFC's borrowing costs fall only as its old bonds and bank loans reprice, typically over two or three quarters. And a single rating downgrade can raise the cost of every new rupee overnight. Cost of funds is the line where a lender's reputation turns into money.

Then the operating cost. Small-ticket lending is labour-intensive: branches in small towns, staff at dealerships, collectors on motorcycles. Two lenders with identical margins can earn very different returns simply because one runs its branches more efficiently. Cost-to-income, operating costs as a share of income, is how you see that.

Then credit cost, the provisions for loans that will not come back. This line is the whole game for a retail NBFC. High yields mean nothing if the borrowers paying them default. The test of a great lender is not how fast it grows in a boom; it is what its credit cost does when the boom ends.

The government infrastructure lenders are the mirror image. Their spread is thin, their costs are tiny, because a handful of offices can manage a book of giant loans, and their credit cost depends on whether states make their power utilities pay on time. Since the late-payment rules of 2022 forced utilities to clear old dues, that question has had a much happier answer.

A retail NBFC earns its margin in the branch and loses it in the field. A government lender earns it in the bond market and loses it in a state capital.
c4.read:
The two charts walk a hundred rupees of revenue, mostly interest earned, down to profit, for the two doors that look most different. Compare them bar by bar.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is interest paid on borrowings. For retail and vehicle lenders it takes roughly four of every ten rupees. For government infrastructure lenders it takes about two thirds. That is the yield gap: retail loans earn far more per rupee lent, so the borrowing bill is a smaller share.
  • The opex bar is where the two charts part company. For retail lenders it takes more than a fifth: branches, staff, collections, technology. For government lenders it is a sliver, because a few large loans need very few people.
  • The third bite is labelled depreciation and interest, but interest is already in the input bar. For a lender, read it as provisions for bad loans plus a little depreciation. It is clearly bigger in the retail chart, which is the price of lending to riskier borrowers.
  • The last bar is profit. Notice that the government lender keeps a slightly larger share of its revenue. That surprises people, and it shows why this chart is not the whole picture: a government lender's revenue per rupee of loans is much smaller, so its profit per rupee of loans is smaller too. That is the medium bar on card one.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes; hover a bar for the amount. Below, the lines list margin, cost of funds, interest, credit cost and opex as yeses, capital as a sometimes, and depreciation and working capital as noes. In a lender, the asset-liability maturity match plays the working-capital role.

c5.story:
The NBFC cycle is not driven by demand. There is always someone who wants a loan. It is driven by two things: whether lenders will lend to the lenders, and whether borrowers pay back. When both are easy, NBFCs grow fast. When either breaks, the weakest go under.

The last full cycle is a textbook case. From 2014, mutual funds were flush with money and happy to buy short-term commercial paper from NBFCs. That cheap, short money funded long loans to home buyers, property developers and consumers. Housing finance companies in particular grew at a blistering pace. It worked as long as the commercial paper could be rolled over every few months.

In September 2018, IL&FS, a large infrastructure lender carrying top ratings, defaulted. Overnight, mutual funds stopped rolling over NBFC paper. Lenders that had borrowed short to lend long found they could not refinance. DHFL collapsed in 2019 and became the first financial company to go through the insolvency code; Piramal took it over in 2021. Then Covid arrived with a loan moratorium and fears of a default wave.

The bottom came in 2020 and 2021, and the way out was telling. Government credit guarantees and RBI liquidity schemes reopened funding. Strong, well-rated lenders found they could borrow when weaker rivals could not, and they took market share. The crisis did what crises do: it consolidated the industry around the survivors.

Since then the cycle has been shaped by the regulator. A boom in 2022 and 2023, the RBI tightening on consumer loans and acting against individual lenders in 2024, rate cuts and partial easing in 2025. Now funding costs are falling, microfinance stress is fading and growth is back.

NBFCs do not die from bad loans first. They die from not being able to borrow, and the bad loans finish the job.
c5.read:
Three parts: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years are the last full funding cycle: the commercial-paper boom of 2014 to 2018, the IL&FS peak of 2018, the bust from 2018 to 2020, and the guarantee-led bottom of 2020 and 2021. Note how short the peak is: a single year, because the turn came as one default rather than a slow fade. The arrow sits just short of the top, at the end of the bottom arc and about to cross into boom: early up-cycle. Hover an arc for its story.

The timeline runs from 2019. The colours give the tone: a bust-coloured 2019 as DHFL fails, a neutral Covid stretch, a boom-coloured 2022 and 2023 under the new scale-based rules, a bust-coloured 2024 when the RBI tightened and microfinance defaults rose, a neutral 2025 as rates fell and gold loans boomed, and 2026 marked now.

The four hands are the readings that move the arrow.

  • Cost of funds: falling with a lag, arrow up. Rate cuts reach NBFC margins two to three quarters later, so the best of this effect is still ahead.
  • Unsecured and microfinance defaults: easing, arrow up.
  • Loan growth: reviving, arrow up. Watch for growth so fast that standards loosen.
  • Gold price: high, a mixed arrow. High gold lifts gold loan books, but a sharp fall would force margin calls and auctions.

Three hands pointing up and one mixed is about as good as this clock gets. The so-what tells you who gains most: well-rated, diversified retail lenders, ahead of pure microfinance and unsecured specialists.

c6.story:
If banks live by the policy rate, NBFCs live by the price of borrowed money in all its forms. Three dials carry three dots each, and every one of them is about funding or rules.

The first is the RBI's policy rate together with system liquidity. Since an NBFC borrows everything, a rate rise raises its costs across the board, and unlike a bank it has no cheap savings accounts to cushion the blow. The direction is clear: a rise hurts. The effect is slow, because borrowings reprice as they mature, which is why NBFCs keep benefiting from rate cuts long after banks have stopped.

The second is corporate bond spreads, the extra interest an NBFC pays over a government bond. In calm markets the spread is narrow and predictable. In a crisis it widens violently, as it did after IL&FS, and spreads are the fastest way to see the market losing confidence in the sector. The third is the RBI's rulebook on risk weights and lending. When the RBI raised risk weights on consumer loans and on bank lending to NBFCs in November 2023, it raised costs twice for an NBFC: once on its own consumer book, and again because banks charged more to lend to it.

Then come the dials that matter for one door more than the others. Gold for the gold lenders. Vehicle sales and freight activity for vehicle financiers, because a truck owner who has loads to carry pays his EMI. Government bond yields for the infrastructure lenders, whose long bonds are priced off them. Rural income and the monsoon for microfinance, tractor and gold loan repayment. Power sector capex for PFC and REC, whose loan books grow with every new plant and transmission line.

Inflation sits in the background with one dot: it decides how much room the RBI has and squeezes household budgets.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches NBFC profits. Most channels on this table run through the liability side: cost of bank loans and bonds, bond spreads, capital needed.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow means a rise helps, a red down arrow means it hurts. There is no diamond on this table, which is unusual: every dial points one way. The policy rate, bond spreads, risk weights, bond yields and inflation are red. Gold, vehicle sales, rural income and power capex are green.
  • Weight: one to three dots. The three three-dot rows are all red, and they are all about the price or availability of funding.

The last column shows today's reading where a series is tracked: the money market rate, our credit spread indicator, the gold price, the auto index as a stand-in for vehicle sales, a government bond fund for yields, consumer prices and electricity output. Risk weights and the monsoon show a dash; for those, read RBI circulars and the monsoon reports.

The way to use this table is to split it in two. The top three rows decide the sector's tide: when rates, spreads and rules are all easing, every NBFC floats. The middle rows decide which door rides it best: a gold rally favours the gold lenders, strong vehicle sales favour the vehicle financiers, a power capex push favours PFC and REC. The so-what says it plainly: track the rate with liquidity, and bond spreads.

c7.story:
The NBFC story has a recurring plot twist: a lender grows fast for years, looks brilliant, and then disappears in a matter of months. The bottlenecks explain why, and the first one explains most of it.

No deposit base. Most NBFCs cannot take public deposits, so they depend entirely on banks and bond investors. Those lenders are fair-weather friends. In good times they compete to fund NBFCs; in a panic they all step back at once. That is a structural feature, not a bad patch, and it is why the market values even excellent NBFCs differently from banks.

The second makes the first deadly: the asset-liability mismatch. If you borrow money for three months and lend it for fifteen years, you are fine only as long as someone keeps rolling over your three-month money. IL&FS and DHFL did exactly that, and when the rollover stopped, so did they. The RBI now watches maturity gaps closely and has pushed larger NBFCs to hold liquidity buffers.

The third is the regulator itself, which has become far more active. In 2024 the RBI barred IIFL Finance from new gold loans, stopped JM Financial from financing share offerings, and later barred several lenders, including a Manappuram microfinance subsidiary, over pricing practices. A year earlier it had stopped Bajaj Finance from lending through two of its digital products for several months. None of these was fatal. All of them hit growth and the stock the day they landed.

Then the credit cycles: unsecured and microfinance lending grows fast, borrowers take loans from too many lenders, and a default wave follows every few years. State politics adds its own twist. Andhra Pradesh's microfinance ordinance in 2010 nearly destroyed that industry, and Karnataka's ordinance in 2025 against coercive recovery disrupted collections again.

Before admiring an NBFC's loan growth, ask who is lending to it and for how long. The answer has ended more NBFCs than bad borrowers ever did.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites and a severity label. Use the label to decide where each risk lives in your process.

  • Structural: the missing deposit base. It never goes away, so it belongs in your valuation. An NBFC will always trade with a funding discount compared with a bank of similar quality.
  • Recurring: the asset-liability mismatch, RBI regulatory tightening and state lending laws. Three of the seven rows are recurring, which tells you this is a sector of frequent shocks. These deserve a news alert per company you own: RBI supervisory actions in particular land without warning.
  • Cyclical: unsecured and microfinance credit cycles. They come in waves every few years and are visible early in bureau data.
  • Two-sided: bank competition. Banks with cheaper money move into gold, vehicle and home loans once those segments look safe, which squeezes NBFC margins. But banks also lend to NBFCs and buy their loan pools, so a healthy banking sector is part of the NBFC funding chain.
  • Slow: state utility finances, the infrastructure lenders' risk. It has been improving gradually since the late-payment rules forced utilities to clear dues.

The so-what line gives the order of inspection. The first two rows, funding dependence and the maturity mismatch, are what turn a slowdown into a collapse. So for any NBFC, read the liability side of the balance sheet, who lends, at what tenor, how much liquidity is held, before you read the loan growth. Most investors do it the other way round.

c8.story:
For most of their history, NBFCs were lightly regulated. The thinking was simple: they did not take public deposits, so their failure would hurt their lenders, not ordinary savers. IL&FS and DHFL ended that thinking. Their collapse showed that a big enough NBFC can freeze the bond market, wound mutual funds and leave banks with large losses. The RBI's answer has been to treat the largest NBFCs more and more like banks.

The centrepiece is scale-based regulation, introduced in 2021 and in force from 2022. It sorts NBFCs into layers by size and risk. The biggest sit in the upper layer and face rules close to a bank's: tighter capital, governance and disclosure, and a requirement to list on the stock exchange. That last rule is why Bajaj Housing Finance listed in 2024 and Tata Capital in 2025. A regulation created two of the market's large recent listings.

Risk weights are the RBI's steering wheel. In November 2023 it raised the capital needed for consumer loans and for bank lending to NBFCs, cooling unsecured growth without banning anything. In 2025 it partly restored them. The gold loan norms, drafted and finalised in 2025, set common rules on how much can be lent against jewellery and how gold is valued and auctioned. The digital lending guidelines decide how NBFCs may work with fintech apps.

Some rules are tools for lenders. The SARFAESI Act lets secured lenders seize collateral without going to court first, which is why a housing or property loan recovers better than an unsecured one. The National Housing Bank refinances and supervises housing finance companies. Expected credit loss accounting under Ind AS already makes large NBFCs provide early in a downturn, ahead of banks, which only adopt it from 2027.

And then there are the states, which can rewrite microfinance recovery rules with a single ordinance.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why it matters, and its status.

  • Always: the RBI as supervisor, the National Housing Bank, the SARFAESI Act and expected-loss accounting. Permanent machinery. Note the RBI row's reason: it can bar a lender from new loans overnight, which is the most dangerous power on this table.
  • Live: scale-based regulation, risk weights, digital lending guidelines and state microfinance laws. These are the rules actively shaping growth and margins today. Risk weights in particular have moved in both directions within two years.
  • New: the gold loan norms. They change how much a gold lender can lend per gram and how it must value and auction, so read them against each gold lender's existing practice.

There is no coming row on this table, which is a small piece of good news: the big structural changes for NBFCs have already happened, unlike for banks, which still face expected-loss provisioning.

The quickest way to use the table is to ask which way each live rule last moved. Right now the answer is mostly loosening: risk weights partly restored, rates falling. That is the third tick in the rule on card eleven. The rulebook's lesson, though, is that the RBI tightens as fast as it loosens, so treat a loosening rule as a tailwind with a short lease.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab. RBI press releases on supervisory action are the ones to read the same day.

c9.story:
Run Michael Porter's five forces over NBFCs and you get two completely different pictures, which is why the card draws two shapes. Who keeps the money depends on which door you stand behind.

For the retail and vehicle lenders, the biggest pressure comes from suppliers. Their suppliers are the banks and bond investors who lend them money, and those suppliers set the price and can walk away. Rivalry is fierce too: banks, fintechs and other NBFCs all want the good borrower, and the entry bar is lower than banking, because an NBFC licence is far easier to get than a bank licence. Every few years a new wave of app-based lenders arrives.

So how do retail NBFCs keep high profits with all that pressure? The answer is the buyer. A truck owner, a shopkeeper or a shopper at a dealership rarely shops around on rate. He cares about speed, convenience and whether the lender understands his situation. Bajaj Finance's real moat is not its rate; it is that the loan is approved at the counter in minutes. Weak buyer power is what pays for everything else.

For the government infrastructure lenders, the picture flips. Suppliers have almost no power, because PFC, REC and IRFC borrow nearly like the government itself. New entrants are close to impossible: nobody enters this business without a sovereign-like rating. Rivalry is a small club of state-owned lenders. But the buyer is powerful. A state power utility or the railways negotiates hard, borrows in huge amounts and can turn to banks or the bond market instead. IRFC's model makes the point: it lends to one customer, the railways, at a margin that customer effectively decides.

A retail NBFC is squeezed from behind and protected in front. A government lender is protected from behind and squeezed in front.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: retail and vehicle lenders, and government infrastructure lenders. Unlike many industries where one shape simply sits inside the other, these two cross, and the crossing is the lesson.

  • The retail shape reaches further on rivalry, supplier and new entrants. Banks and bond investors control its funding, and fintechs keep arriving.
  • The government shape reaches further on exactly one spoke, buyer, where it scores near the top. Its handful of state customers bargain hard.
  • On substitutes, both sit at moderate, with retail a touch higher: banks, payment apps and buy-now-pay-later services stand in for retail loans.

Notice the near-zero spoke: new entrants for government lenders. It is the lowest score on the chart and the reason this door is safe.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a reason. Use it to adjust for a specific company. A retail NBFC with a top rating and a parent group, such as a Bajaj or a Tata company, deserves a shorter supplier spoke than the average. A small unrated lender deserves a longer one. The so-what line ties it back: retail NBFCs with niche customers and good collections keep the most; government lenders keep a thin, safe spread and pay it out as dividends.

c10.story:
An NBFC's quarterly presentation will tell you about new branches, digital customer counts and product launches. Skip to eight numbers, and read them in pairs, because in lending every number lies a little when read alone.

Start with AUM growth, assets under management, which for a lender simply means the loan book. Fast growth is the headline everyone quotes. But growth is the easiest number to manufacture: lower your standards and borrowers will queue up. So read it next to credit cost, the provisions set aside for bad loans. Growth with stable credit cost is skill. Growth with rising credit cost is a bill that arrives in a year.

Next, the net interest margin with the cost of funds. The margin tells you the spread; the cost of funds tells you whether that spread is about to widen or narrow. For a top-rated lender, the cost of funds should sit close to the best corporate bond rates. A lender paying well above that is being told something by its own lenders.

Then gross defaulted loans, the stock of loans already in trouble, measured under Ind AS as stage three loans. Pair it with cost to income, operating costs as a share of income, because collection-heavy businesses can hide stress in rising costs before it shows up as defaults.

Finally, the outcome and the cushion: return on assets, the cleanest measure of quality, and capital adequacy, the room to grow before raising equity. A lender with a high return on assets and ample capital can fund its own growth; one with thin capital will be back asking shareholders for money.

In lending, growth is the claim and credit cost is the evidence.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question each number answers, from book growth to spread, funding, credit quality, efficiency, profit and capital.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures, and it nearly always gives two benchmarks, one for retail lenders and one for infrastructure lenders. Respect the split. A government lender with a margin in the low single digits is perfectly healthy; a consumer lender with the same margin would be in trouble.
  • Today's industry median shows a dash on every row. That is expected: our medians come from standard filing lines, which do not carry lender metrics like margin, credit cost or capital adequacy. For NBFCs these come from the quarterly investor presentation.

So treat the table as a checklist. For each NBFC you own, fill in the eight numbers from its latest presentation and read them in the pairs from the story: growth with credit cost, margin with cost of funds, bad loans with cost to income, return on assets with capital.

Watch the first row's wording, too. The good mark for AUM growth carries a condition: without credit cost rising. That condition is the most important phrase in the whole table. A lender that clears the growth bar while breaking the condition is not passing; it is borrowing profit from next year.

c11.story:
Most of what decides an NBFC's next two quarters is visible in public data before the company reports. The trick is to know which voices speak early.

The same-quarter signals are blunt. The gold price moves gold loan books in real time: a higher price means each gram supports a bigger loan. An RBI circular raising risk weights or barring a lender hits growth the day it lands.

One quarter ahead, three signals matter. Corporate bond and commercial paper spreads show funding stress before results do; in 2018 the spreads blew out before the defaults were fully understood. Monthly vehicle sales drive vehicle finance disbursements a quarter later. And microfinance collection efficiency, the share of dues actually collected each month, falls before defaults are recognised.

Two quarters ahead sit the slow but powerful signals. The RBI's policy rate and liquidity reach NBFC borrowing costs over two to three quarters, as old borrowings mature and are replaced. Credit bureau delinquency data, early late payments on consumer and microfinance loans, lead credit costs by about the same distance.

Put them together and the rule is straightforward. NBFCs are in an up-cycle when funding costs are falling, credit costs are stable or easing, and the RBI is loosening rather than tightening. Today all three hold: rate cuts are passing through, microfinance stress is fading, and risk weights have been partly restored. That is the best reading this rule can give.

But notice the warning built into the rule's own wording: the regulator can reverse the last sign quickly. Three ticks is a good place to be and a bad place to get complacent. The call is constructive, with a preference for well-rated diversified lenders over the specialists that were hit hardest in 2024.

The chart places outside signals by lead time. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for the channel.

  • Far left, same quarter: the gold price, and RBI circulars on risk weights and supervisory action.
  • Middle, one quarter ahead: corporate bond and commercial paper spreads, monthly vehicle sales, microfinance collection efficiency.
  • Right, two quarters ahead: the RBI policy rate and liquidity, and credit bureau delinquency data.

Read the chart right to left each quarter: rates and bureau data first, because they set the quarter after next; then spreads, vehicles and collections; then the same-quarter dots to confirm.

Below the chart, the rule shows three signs. Funding costs falling: a tick, rate cuts passing through. Credit costs easing: a tick, microfinance stress fading. RBI loosening: a tick, risk weights partly restored. Three out of three is the full reading, and you will not see it often.

The call box then gives the view, constructive, with its points and what would change it: a funding shock or a large default widening bond spreads, a fresh rise in unsecured or microfinance defaults, or a sharp fall in gold. Map each alert to a dot on the chart: spreads, bureau data and the gold price. That is the practical use of this card. The dots tell you which alert will fire first, and the spreads dot, one quarter ahead, is the one that has fired first in every NBFC crisis so far.
